utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, The Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer; Sarah Clanton; Thomas Laugel; legal intern, Kai Hong Leung.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. GH-145. Is that it, Mr. Stringer, or Ms. Clanton?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good Morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I take it your testimony will be in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please state your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Aernout van Lynden. I was born on the 31st of December, 1954.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. van Lynden you are about to make the solemn declaration, by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I have to point out to you that by doing so you commit -- you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to this Court. May I now ask you to take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Ms. Clanton, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Do you recall giving a statement to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor in May of this year?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would like to ask for the assistance of the Registry, please, to pull up 65 ter 06425, statement dated 24th of May, 2013. This is at tab number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. van Lynden, do you recognise this as the statement that you gave to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And could you please look at the signature on the bottom right of the English version. Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Bottom right. That would be yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Bottom left. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That would be mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If we could now turn to the last page of the statement, which is page 36 in e-court. Now do you recognise the signature at the bottom right of this page?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And since your signed this statement in May, have you had an opportunity to review it?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And if I were to ask you the same questions today, as I asked at the time that you gave your statement, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I would hope so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And now that you've taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the accuracy and truthfulness of your statement?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 06425 into evidence along with the associated exhibits, pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2333, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, with the usher's assistance, I would like to provide a hard copy of the statement to the witness. If the Defence would like to look at it that's fine, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. van Lynden, I would like to start today by asking you a few additional questions about your professional background. In your statement in paragraph 7 you stated that before you became a journalist you were a member of the Royal Netherlands Marine Corps. What specific training did you receive?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I served in the Dutch marine corps as a reservist. We had still national service in this country. I did one year officer training and then served for just over a year as a second lieutenant, so that was general infantry training as a platoon commander and separately to that once I had become a second lieutenant I was given mortar platoon training as a commander of mortar platoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And then I understand from your statement at paragraph 8 that you worked as a war correspondent for roughly 23 years and then in 2001 when you left Sky News.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: How are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm employed by Leiden university as a lecturer at Leiden University College here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And when did you begin working there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I began working at Leiden University College two years ago.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly requested to make pauses between question and answer for the purpose of interpretation because this pace is impossible to interpreter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I apologise as well to the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, what subjects do you teach at Leiden University College The Hague?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I teach courses in war studies and in journalism.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And now I have a preliminary question concerning the video-clips that form part of your statement. To avoid any confusion later, can you tell the Chamber who is the person speaking in all of the Sky News clips that we reviewed and that form part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: You're referring to myself, to my voice over.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to turn back to 1991. And at paragraph 24 of your statement you've described that in the late summer and in the early Autumn, you travelled regularly from Belgrade to the front lines in eastern Croatia. You've said that you followed two different routes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would like to ask for the Registrar's assistance, please, to pull up 65 ter 01927. This is ERN 07066872, and it's a map of north western Serbia and eastern Croatia, and it appears at tab number 44. And I would like to ask for the usher's assistance, please, to provide Mr. van Lynden with the pen in order to mark the map. Now -- Mr. van Lynden, this map does not show Belgrade but are you able to mark for the Chamber the southern route that you followed into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. We would come along this road to a place called Sid, then continue to Oriolik and then go up past Negoslavci into Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And while we still have this map, can you tell the Chamber, please, what you recall about the route that you took when you travelled into Croatia via the northern route.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Then we would -- where precisely the road -- I imagine is this road from Belgrade. How we precisely drove, I -- but we would then take the road to here, and here there is a bridge across the river Danube, Your Honour, to the place of Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would like to tender this map as marked into evidence, please, 65 ter 01927.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2334, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. We could make the map down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, in paragraph 9 of your statement, you've indicated that you returned to Belgrade every day after reporting in eastern Croatia. How frequently were you required to sent a story to your office in London?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Basically every single day. Sky News was 24-hour news channel so basically I had 24 deadlines a day, what one could have on certain days, but certainly one story a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you're reporting during the war in Croatia from Belgrade, what did you observe about the coverage of the war by the local television networks?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Basically in 1991 you had the state broadcaster, Belgrade television. We were actually based inside it and we had a room inside Belgrade television where we could edit our material and that was also the -- what we call the feed point by satellite of our story to London. So I did see quite a bit of what was going -- being put out on Belgrade television. Of course, it had to be translated to me. I do not speak Serbo-Croat. But I had both a producer in Belgrade and a field producer who came into the field with me, both of them were Yugoslavs. They would translate for me and what we basically heard was night after night when I would call an incitement to hatred, saying that the Serbs were threatened by what was usually called the Ustashi, a reference to the Fascist Croat state during the Second World War, and this -- this threat and the pictures were often -- that were often shown were indeed those of the past of the fighting and the massacres that had taken place during the Second World War. Later on, of course, when the fighting really broke out in Croatia they would show pictures of that fighting going on, but they always made it clear that they felt that they were fighting a Fascist Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. The next topic that I would like to ask you about is what you saw and what you experienced when you travelled on the southern route that you've just marked for the Judges. In your statement, at paragraph 26, you've described how you needed two passes each day to access Croatia via the highway from Belgrade: First, from the Ministry of Defence in Belgrade and another in Sid. When you were in Sid, can you tell us who you met with?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: A small office had been set up manned by three or four people from the Ministry of Defence. As far as I recall, a couple of guys, and a couple of ladies. And we would -- I don't remember the -- precisely whether we needed to get a second pass or we needed to get our pass from Belgrade stamped but we certainly had to pass by the office and show that we did have a pass -- had gotten a pass the previous evening from the Ministry of Defence in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the people that you've described who worked in this office related to the pass that you had received or had stamped in Sid, do you recall if you met with any particular people when you were in Sid?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not really. Not in Sid, no. Outside of Sid, we -- we were on one -- on several occasions brought to one of the JNA Yugoslav army generals, General Arandjelovic. But he was not in Sid itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would like to ask the assistance of Mr. Laugel, please, to play a video-clip. This clip has 65 ter number 05030.6. It is an excerpt of the video bearing ERN V000-4590. The clip runs from 34 minutes and 3 seconds to 36 minutes and 23 seconds. There's a Sky News report and an associated exhibit and it can be found at tab number 35. And I would like to for Mr. Laugel to play this and pause at the time code at 34 minutes and 16 seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: "Major-General Arandjelovic, field commander on the Vukovar front explains how and where a relief column will be let through his lines to the besieged Croat forces inside the strategic town ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. van Lynden, can you tell us who you recognise in this still at 34 minutes and 16 seconds?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: A somewhat younger version of myself and Major-General Arandjelovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. van Lynden, [indiscernible] Arandjelovic just mentioned to you that there would be a relief column. I'd like to ask that other than the topic of relief columns what were the other subjects of your discussions with General Arandjelovic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: What the situation on the ground was, as far as the fighting was concerned, and for us personally to get access to those front lines. This was not the first time that we met the general. These pictures that you have just shown. And the first time we saw him we asked him about the deployment of Yugoslav army troops, of the state of the battle, and then we asked him about personal access for us to the front lines. He gave it. The very first time we met him he actually saw to it that an armoured car, that we were put into one of his armoured cars to be taken to the front line where fighting was still taking place. That was the village of Ilaca which was then still -- where the houses were still burning, so it had only just been taken. On other occasions including this one, when we met him - this is much later - he said yes we would have access to the front lines and also be able to actually see this relief column enter Vukovar and we were stopped in Negoslavci by a much lower officer who said that we could not continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could actually now play this video-clip to 34 minutes and 45 seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: "... in Eastern Slavonia. "The army sticks to the cease-fire and wants to do what we agreed with the Croats, so today we will enable them to take a convoy of food, medicine, and fuel into Vukovar and take out their sick and wounded. "At high speed under military escort, we are taken to the front line village where the general has arranged for the relief convoy to cross army lines. Just outside Vukovar, we are stopped and told a different story."

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. van Lynden, I briefly just explained to the Chamber about the time that General Arandjelovic told you about this convoy and that you were stopped. Can you confirm the name of the village in this footage?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We were in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And how frequently did this occur, that you had a pass from the Ministry of Defence in Belgrade and that it had been acknowledged or supplemented in Sid but that you were still stopped on the road?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, we were always stopped because there were check-points. What we didn't know is whether we were going to get through the check-points. Even with the general's permission sometimes we were stopped, other points we were let through. It was an uncertainty every single day we went to Vukovar and there were several days that we did not get to the front line simply because we were stopped and no particular reason was given to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And in this footage that we've just seen, you said that you had an army escort. I would like to know if you were aware of any journalist who travelled to the front lines with any other armed groups?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. Other journalists from Belgrade did go to the front lines around Vukovar with paramilitary units, not with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And now turning to what you told us a moment ago about Ilaca, you mentioned to the Chamber - and this in paragraph 27 and 28 of your statement as well - that you went through Ilaca and in your statement it also says Tovarnik. I want to ask you what did you observe in these towns, or villages, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That there had been heavy fighting, that considerable damage had been done to practically every house. Certain houses were completely burnt out. Other houses had been at least partially destroyed by heavier gun-fire, probably from tanks. That there were -- was no one living there anymore. No more civilians. And, as I said earlier, in Ilaca, the houses were actually still burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would like to ask for Mr. Laugel's assistance again, please, to pull up a video-clip that is 65 ter 05030.5. This is an excerpt of the same video but with time code 15:37 to 18 minutes and the Sky News report as well and an associated exhibit which can be found at tab 34.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, I've been asked to pause between the end of the clip and my question so that the transcript can catch up so that's why I will taking a brief pause.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And I would like for Mr. Laugel to pause at the time code at 16 minutes and 2 seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: "Some of them head straight for the front. Heavy armour and lines of civilian trucks carrying logistics for an army which is once again reinforcing its forces on the front lines of eastern Croatia. They pass through the ruins of Tovarnik, a mixed village which fell into Serb hands a week ago. Although ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, in the clip that we just saw, you said that the village was in ruins and that it fell into Serb hands one week prior. From the time that you spent in this village, can you tell us who you heard was responsible for it the attack on Tovarnik?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was -- I don't think anybody told us any differently. It had been attacked by the JNA and the Serb territorials.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And do you know where it was attacked from?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I imagine from -- from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, again, in paragraph 27 of your statement, you commented that you saw destruction in Ilaca, which we saw in the video-clip, Oriolik and Negoslavci. I would like to ask you to describe the degree of destruction in Negoslavci compared to what you saw in the other towns.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In Tovarnik the destruction was severe. Where you have halted the video, this is one of the two churches, Your Honours, in Tovarnik and both the churches had been destroyed. And the destruction was widespread to the houses. In the next village, that is Ilaca, towards Vukovar, as I said earlier, all houses -- or all the houses -- most of the houses were burning when we actually arrived there. The village had only just a day or so before fallen into the hands of the JNA. As we got closer to Vukovar, the destruction was not as severe. In the village of Oriolik and Negoslavci, as far as I recall today, yes, there were signs that there had been fighting but there was nothing like the destruction that we had seen in Tovarnik and Ilaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now if I could ask for Mr. Laugel's assistance, I would like to play the same clip again but starting at 16:30 and to time code 16:45, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: "Further from the fronts at corps HQ, the last Serb reservists to be mobilised are unloaded from a bus. An unhappy looking bunch, they realise as does their general the kind of war they'll be engaged in."

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, in this clip, you've said that you're filming further from the front at the corps HQ, and we see the buses with reservists who you indicated have come from Serbia. Are you able to tell the Chamber where this is being filmed?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This was in, as far as I recall, in -- in Serbia, near -- near Sid.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And you've stated that the general of these men talked to you about the fighting that they would be engaged in. Who is the general?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The general that you see here is the same general we saw before, General Arandjelovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This is my first meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 25 of your statement you've described crossing into Croatia at Erdut and going to a grain silo that had been captured near the village of Brsadin. I'd like to know for the Chamber, please, how did you get directions to travel from Erdut to this silo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We indeed crossed over the bridge and the Danube from Serbia into Croatia at -- at the town of Erdut. There, we passed by the office of the defendant and I introduced my field producer to him. We met up with local journalists, and I cannot today recall precisely who informed us that the grain silo had fallen into Serb hands, and -- but someone did and said they would take us there and we went with a few local journalists and, as I recall, members what were called the Territorial Defence forces and -- were driven to the silo and filmed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And can you briefly describe for the Chamber the significance of the taking of this grain silo for the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Eastern Slavonia, Your Honours, is flat, and, therefore, a grain silo of this size means that you have captured the high ground, particularly important for artillery observers who could then bring in fire on various targets that otherwise would not be seen with more precision.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would like to ask for Mr. Laugel's assistance again, please, to play the video-clip that is 65 ter number 05030.4. This is once again an excerpt of the video with the ERN number V000-4590. It runs from 6 minutes and 29 seconds to 8 minutes and 38 seconds. This is also a Sky News report and an associated exhibit which is at tab 33. And I would like for Mr. Laugel to please play from the beginning and then pause at 7 minutes and 7 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: "The giant grain silo on the edge of the town of Borovo Naselje. Cease-fire or no cease-fire, it is the larges conquest of the Serbs, a crucial one. The silo forms the high-ground on the battle field of eastern Croatia. On Monday it was still in the hands of the Croats, and now after a brief fierce fight, it's the Serb snipers whose eyes roam over the whole terrain of their foes now besieged on practically all sides. As ever, both sides blame the other for this latest violation of Sunday's brittle truce. And sporadically the ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. van Lynden, in this still at 7 minutes and 7 seconds, can you identify, please, the towns and villages that have visible?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This is Borovo Naselje and Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And if Mr. Laugel could please now play to the end of the clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: "... violations continue. As do the preparations for further fire-fights in days ahead. "With their capture of this strategic point, these village militiamen have made it all too clear that they have no belief in the current cease-fire, and no real wish to abide by it. For them the fall of Borovo Naselje has been postponed, but in their opinion, only very temporarily. "Most of the militiamen are locals, an unlikely collection of old and young inhabitants of the neighbouring village of Brsadin, who, their duty on the front line done, return home with a strange mixture of acquisitions. Others scan the grounds for booby-traps and mines, finding several of the latter, disposing of them in time-honoured fashion - length of fuse attached to dynamite, and ignited by a match. "In Brsadin, the mood is surprising relaxed. These farmers turned militiamen waiting for the battle to recommence, none of them doubts that it will, and that with the capture of the silo, the Serbian's noose around the Croats of Borovo Naselje has been tightened another crucial notch, making the fate of the town a deadly certainty. "Aernout van Lynden, Sky News."

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, in this last segment you've commented on the village militiamen who you encountered who were of various ages and occupations. How common was it for you to encounter armed Serb groups of a similar composition in the villages that you travelled through?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: My experience is that there was a difference in the people that I encountered on the northern route into the battle of Borovo Naselje and Vukovar and on the southern route. On the southern route it was basically, although not solely, but basically the JNA, although we did at certain moments see paramilitary units as well. On the northern route it was a mixture. There were JNA officers there and JNA soldiers but there were also Territorial Defence and paramilitaries as well. It was more of a mix on the northern than on the southern one.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to ask you what types of heavy weaponry that you saw being used against Borovo Naselje and Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, in a previous clip, you saw a tank driving through Tovarnik on its way to Vukovar and there were tanks of various sorts deployed around Vukovar and Borovo Naselje. Aside from that, there was heavy artillery of various calibres which we also filmed, multiple-rocket-launchers, heavy mortars, 120-millimetre mortars, but also in -- during the fighting in Vukovar itself, we also saw the use of light mortars, 60-millimetre mortars. Really, the whole scalar of what an army has in -- in terms of heavy weaponry was deployed during the siege and fighting for Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If I could ask for Mr. Laugel's assistance again to play video-clip 65 ter number 05030.8. This is from the same video as the prior clip, and it has time code 19:56 to 21 minutes and 12 seconds. This is also a Sky News report and is an associated exhibit which can be found at tab 37. And I would ask for Mr. Laugel to play this video and pause at 20 minutes and 29 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: "More ordinance streaks for the skies bound for the Croatian front lines in Slavonia. Further proof of Yugoslavia's crumbling cease-fire. The rains have no halted the staggering built-up by the federal army, around the besieged Croatian towns of Vukovar and Vinkovci. On the roads which are fast becoming covered by mud, the columns of armoured Jeeps and truck, are almost continuous, and they're heading in only one direction - to the front."

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, at the beginning of the segment we saw repetitive firing and what you said was that this ordnance was bound for the Croatian front lines in Slavonia. What kind of weaponry is being used?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That was multiple-rocket-launcher fire, also known previously as Stalin's Organ. These are a bunch of tubes usually on the back of a truck, and they are capable of -- of this kind of sustained, if not very precise, fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And you've just mentioned that the fire was not very precise from this kind of weapon. Could you elaborate a bit more based on your experience about the impact that's caused by this kind of weaponry?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and the counsel make pauses between questions and answers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This kind of ordinance will -- you cannot target with multiple-rocket-launcher fire a precise target. It hits an area, a rough area. It is specifically effective if once troops are coming under attack from a -- an opposing side, specifically also, of course, an infantry attack. Artillery fire from a -- can be much, much more precise. If can be indeed, if there artillery, observers seeing where the shells land. They can be brought absolutely precisely on one particular target. And that is not possible with multiple-rocket-launcher fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. van Lynden, what did you see or what were you told about return fire from the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I was both told and what I witnessed was that the only return fire and on any occasion was small-arms fire. When we were in Vukovar itself, later on during the battle, the Yugoslav troops that we were with said that they -- one of their biggest problems really was booby-traps, mines, but it was clear from every time that we went to Vukovar that the Croats did not have the kind of heavy weaponry. They had no artillery, and one felt safe and everybody just walked around quite close to the front lines and that is also a signal that there -- the opposing side did not have the kind of heavy weaponry that the Serbs did.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you about the first time that you entered Vukovar in October of 1991. In paragraph 33 of your statement, you've described entering Vukovar and going to the barracks from the southern route and that you were transported there in an armoured personnel carrier. Do you recall who it was who arranged for you to go to the barracks on that day?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That was -- again it was General Arandjelovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And how would you describe the condition of the barracks buildings?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The barracks, Your Honours, had been besieged. This was a Croat tactic throughout Croatia, besieging the barracks of the JNA, of the Yugoslav Army to stop the army from being able to move out of them, and this had also occurred at Vukovar. Whilst we were not in a position because this was a front line and there was shooting going on, small-arms fire, all around, when we arrived there, the barracks basically were -- had not been destroyed and -- and [indiscernible] there were marks of rifle fire but nothing heavier than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If I could ask for Mr. Laugel's assistance to play 65 ter 05030.9. This is part of the same video with the ERN ending in the digits 4590. This clip is from 29 minutes and 44 seconds to 31 minutes and 36 seconds. It's also a Sky News report, an associated exhibit at tab 38. I would like for this clip to be played from the time code 29 minutes and 59 seconds to 30 minutes and 14 seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: "After five days of fierce combat the army has established control only over the south western part of the city. Their barracks once besieged have been relieved and it is in the bunkers there that the battle for the streets above is co-ordinated."

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, in paragraph 37 of your statement, you said that some of the people that you interviewed said that the fighting in Vukovar was being waged in order to liberate the barracks and you said that was done in October of 1991. And so after that point you were not convinced that that was the correct reason for the continuation of the fighting? And I want to ask if you could confirm for the Chamber what it was that you saw that led you to this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Quite simply that the fighting continued. And it -- the -- the -- the barracks, blockade of the barracks had been broken through. But the fighting in Vukovar, the shelling of Vukovar - and this is continual heavy shelling of Vukovar - continued right up until its fall a month later.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now I want to ask you about your experience in Vukovar when you spent the night there from the 12th to the 13th of November, 1991. And this is in paragraph 36 of your statement. In that paragraph, you said that the atmosphere at night was strange and spooky because the Serbs were blaring nationalist Serb music at the Croats to taunt them. Were there lyrics to this music?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I recall, yes there were. It is the only instance, Your Honours, in my whole career that I've been in a war zone where one side starts playing music at the other. It was very eery. It seemed like something out of a -- a film, not a particularly good film. And we were told and I was told also by -- I had my field producer with me who said these were nationalist Serb songs and that they were played to taunt the Croat defenders of Vukovar. We were with a guards unit of the Yugoslav army, and they said that this music was being played by paramilitaries not by the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: The next topic I'd like to ask you about is the events on the morning of the 18th of November, 1991, when you attended a press briefing in Negoslavci. Now this is in paragraph 38 of your statement. And what you've said is that you attended ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam Prosecutor, sorry to interrupt you. I would like to ask a question to the witness. Mr. van Lynden, before moving to the next topic, as Madam Prosecutor just suggested, I would like to come back on what you described earlier on. We've watched several videos showing destructions in Tovarnik, Ilaca, and even in Vukovar. With regard to Tovarnik and Ilaca, on transcript page 12, it was said that houses had been burnt and destroyed, even churches. But, at the same time, you said that heavy fighting was going on, using artillery and heavy artillery weapons. My question is the following: On the basis of your experience, destroying churches and houses, was it due to this heavy fighting or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the heavy fighting in Tovarnik and Ilaca had taken place before I was there. But if you see houses are destroyed and houses are still burning, one reaches the conclusion that the fighting was heavy. Everything that I saw in Eastern Slavonia was that the heavy weaponry, the heavy artillery, the tanks, only belonged to one side, and that the other side did not have such weaponry. So if I see a house that is being destroyed through tank fire, then my conclusion was relatively simple, that that had been done by the JNA rather than by the Croats. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much. For the time being, that will suffice.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, we were speaking about paragraph 38 of your statement and the press briefing that you attended on the 18th of November, 1991, as given by Mr. Sljivancanin. I'd like to ask you what you recall about the language that Mr. Sljivancanin was using during that briefing.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We had arrived in Negoslavci to go to Vukovar. We had not been aware before we arrived there that we would get this briefing and, indeed, that there would be a surrender of Croat forces, but we were stopped in Negoslavci. We knew Mr. Sljivancanin and we were invited to the briefing, and he then explained what was going to happen, or -- and that he -- he -- the other that really we noticed was that he only spoke about the Ustashi. He never spoke about the Croats. And I remember that that struck us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. van Lynden, do you recall if he said anything about the duration of the continuing battle?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I recall, what he said was that either they surrender now or we will destroy them in a matter of hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And I would like for Mr. Laugel to please assist by bringing up video-clip 65 ter 04775.1. This is part of the video with the ERN V000-0625. And this is an excerpt that runs from the beginning of the tape to 16 minutes and 9 seconds. It was not filmed by Sky News, and it is not an associated exhibit. It appears at tab 5, and we're going to play a short excerpt, beginning at 4 minutes and 10 seconds and playing until 5 minutes and 59 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Perhaps to assist the interpreters, I should repeat the 65 ter number: 65 ter 04775.1. And, Mr. Laugel, they've indicated we can start again from the same point, from 4 minutes and 10 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... about the transport of those Ustashas and then we will provide all the vehicles, all the medical aid, and everything necessary for the hospital to be evacuated from Vukovar and that all the other civilians who are being kept by -- as hostages by them be helped. And they are kept in the shelters and in the area of the hospital north of the river Vuka. He replied to us that a possibility exists that there are such extremists who would try to fire at us, at our soldiers. We have warned Mr. Vidic that we will not attack or open fire if he guarantees that our soldiers will not be fired upon. If they resort to any kind of trick or try to do anything outside of what has been agreed, we told him, also, that we will point around 100 artillery weapons directly at them, and we will not spare anything anymore. "Q. You won't spare anyone? "A. No. We will spare the people and the citizens. The Ustashas, no. At this moment, we have such forces and means that in two hours we could also finish off this last job that has to be done."

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, do you recognise the speaker in this clip?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. This is Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And where were you while he was giving this speech?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And we just heard Mr. Sljivancanin say that they could finish this last job which had to be done in two hours. What impression did this speech of his leave on you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It had been clear to us earlier also when we had spent a night in Vukovar on the front lines that the battle was drawing to a close. What he was saying now was that, after basically a three-month siege of the city, that the army was now in a position to finish the whole thing, also militarily, in a couple of hours. Given the enormous overweight of heavy weaponry and of manpower, I had very little doubt that if he had used all of that that there would have been a bloodbath, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 04775.1 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2335, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I ask for some more water, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, later that same day, on the 18th of November, 1991, you stated in paragraph 41 of your statement that you witnessed the departure of several thousands persons, including men, women, and children. Can you tell the Chamber, please, what is the name of the part of Vukovar where these people came from.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I recall being told that they came from the Mitnica area of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And now I'd like to ask to please play a video-clip with 65 ter 04973.2. This is part of the video with ERN V000-6475, and it goes from 12 minutes and 1 seconds to 14 minutes and 10 seconds. And this is a Sky News report and associated exhibit, and appears at tab 24. And I would like for Mr. Laugel to play this clip beginning at 13 minutes and 12 seconds and carrying on to 13 minutes and 22 seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: "Many Croats had feared a massacre but this operation is well run. There's not even any taunting. Federal soldiers looking on in inquisitive silence."

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. van Lynden, on what day did you file this report?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: On the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And in your report, you've stated that there were fears of a massacre. Can you explain why you reported this?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, for two different reasons: Firstly, as we've just heard, one of the army commanders at Vukovar had threatened to bring down, to bear all his heavy weaponry, use it all, against the remaining fighters and -- but also the remaining population in Vukovar; secondly, this was a war between neighbours, people who had -- used to belong in one country where there had already been massacres. And there was a fear, I think, a general fear, amongst all outsiders that if a town like Vukovar fell, that there could well be a massacre of some kind. And we, as outside observers, which is what journalists are, were there also for the reason that we hoped that our mere presence would stop that kind of thing from happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you about the persons that you encountered in the centre of Vukovar on the 19th of November, 1991, and this is at paragraph 44 of your statement. In that paragraph, you've indicated that in the town centre you saw persons who identified themselves as Seselj's men or Chetniks, celebrating in the street. And you also said that close to the hotel there were freshly dead bodies who had been shot. From what you could see from these freshly dead bodies, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And I would like to ask for Mr. Laugel to assist, please, by bringing up the video-clip with 65 ter 05033.3. This is part of the video with the ERN V000-4593 and the clip runs from 12 seconds to 6 minutes and 38 seconds. It is also a Sky News report prepared by Mr. van Lynden and an associated exhibit, which is at tab 39. And I would like to start this clip at 4 minutes and 14 seconds and play to 5 minutes and 29 seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: "Amongst the horror there is the surreal incongruity of celebration, extremist Serb militiaman and women posing triumphantly for an end-of-battle photograph before returning to a morning feast of music and laughter, fueled by alcohol. "The motto on their flag is freedom or death and they vow they will fight on. "No, it is not finished. "What do you, the Serbs need to take before the war is over? "War will be over when we have our limits Karlobag-Karlovac-Ogulin-Virovitica. All places Serbian people live must be free. You know, we must clean up with the Croatians. "In the town centre other militiamen display an uncontrolled rejoicing and a similar frame of mind. But the army's... "

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, in your statement at paragraph 44, you said that you thought that the militias were dangerous. Who do you think they posed a threat to?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Basically anyone. These were undisciplined fighters who were drinking early in the morning. We had kept our distance from such units, and we had -- in going into Vukovar always gone with Yugoslav army and, indeed, in the end, the -- the unit we linked up with was the most professional of the Yugoslav army, the guards, and this is also the unit that we actually stayed with overnight and they said we were 40, 50 metres, sleeping 40, 50 metres from Croat lines. Those were clearly disciplines soldiers with a hierarchy of command. These people who we simply ran into on that morning of the 19th weren't -- by the way, we had first linked up again with the guards unit that we knew. They took us around town, and we saw these people, I thought that they were dangerous. They were shooting in the air, as you saw in -- and they were drinking, and when people who are armed start drinking alcohol, you don't know what they're going do next. So I thought that they were dangerous, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And I think you've touched on this in a previous answer. But I wanted to ask you, related to the same day, in paragraph 45 of your statement, you said that you entered into an informal agreement with Martin Bell of the BBC, that you would not cover the same places on that day, that is, that you would move around separately. Can you describe for the Chamber what factors caused you to reach that inform agreement with Mr. Bell?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I'd known Martin Bell for quite some time already. On the previous day, on the 18th of November, we had been at the same place filming the surrender of Croat forces and of those 4.000 civilians walking out of the Mitnica area of Vukovar. When we spoke at the end, we said when we go into the city tomorrow it's better if we're not at the same place. There weren't very many foreign journalists going into Vukovar and it made sense to us that if we were at different places and civilians came out of there, where they had been hiding, that our presence could stop them from being shot and so we were not in the same areas. I'm aware of at least one instance because Martin and his crew were in a certain place, they were able to intervene and stop a civilian from being shot, and similarly we, at a certain moment, encountered one man in the centre of Vukovar, again wearing civilian clothes, being grabbed by the militiamen of -- who said that they were with Mr. Seselj and we were able to tell Yugoslav army soldiers that they should intervene and they did, and they took that man away. And as I also said we saw dead bodies on the street. So it was -- some people were definitely killed that day after the town had fallen.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And now, Mr. van Lynden, moving to the 20th of November, 1991, in paragraph 49 of your statement, you've described seeing Mr. Sljivancanin and the representative of the ICRC having an argument outside of Vukovar Hospital. You've also stated that the representative of the ICRC took the unusual step of speaking to you on camera about the JNA having breached agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And I would like to ask Mr. Laugel to please pull up 65 ter 04799.1. This is admitted exhibit P1653.1645. Now this is not a Sky News report but it's an associated exhibit at tab 21. And I would like to play this clip which comes from the video with ERN V000-1131 from 2 hours, 26 minutes and 56 seconds to 2 hours, 27 minute and 4 seconds. In this clip, the speakers are speaking Serbian and they're speaking over the English, but it is still possible to hear the English in the background if you listen very carefully and have good hearing. For this reason, I would like to ask that the English booth not read the transcript so that the witness can listen to the original recording, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. van Lynden, in that very short clip were you able to recognise the voice that's asking a question in English?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I think that was my voice.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, in addition, in your statement, you've indicated that you were present when Mr. Sljivancanin gave a speech to the cameras about his disagreement with the ICRC representative. How would you describe the relations between the two men at this point?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: They were very angry with each other. Mr. Sljivancanin said that the ICRC representative wouldn't -- couldn't understand that this was a situation of war and on the ICRC part, Mr. -- I think he was called Borsinger said that there had been an agreement reached with various parties but that the behaviour of the Yugoslav army in Vukovar itself made it impossible for him to do his work for the ICRC to do their work.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you did observe the eventually evacuation of the persons from the Vukovar Hospital onto buses, can you describe the demographic composition of that group?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, they were wounded, and then it was mostly women and children, some elderly. But what I think you're asking about, were there a lot of young men, no there were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And the people that you saw, the women, the children, some elderly, as you indicated, what was your impression of their well-being at that time?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, this comes at the end of a siege of their town of three months. These people were still extremely frightened and they were traumatised. Many had lived in almost inhumane conditions in the basement of the hospital. We had visited the basement of the hospital on the previous day. The sanitary situation there was appalling. They were probably being ill-fed during all this time, although they hadn't actually starved. And they knew that they were leaving their town, and, at that moment, they thought that they were leaving their town, which was the town of their birth, forever.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a question about the buildings and the condition of the town of Vukovar itself. When you entered Vukovar previously - that is, on the 12th and 13th of November, 1991 - you reported that the city was decimated and this is in paragraph 36 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask for Mr. Laugel to please play the video-clip 65 ter 04775.3. This is part of the video V000-0625, and this is raw footage not taken by Sky News and not an associated exhibit. It's available at tab 39. And, Your Honours, we're playing this solely for the images. So if we could please have no sound. And to start the clip at 1 minute and 14 seconds and play until 2 minutes and 40 seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, do you recognise the streets and the buildings shown in this footage?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I couldn't name you the name of the streets, but, yes, this is the centre of Vukovar that I saw trees pruned by shell fire. You don't do that with rifles. That is -- you can only have trees knocked down like that if there has been heavy shell fire. It's reminiscent of scenes from the First World War that we've seen in photographs and paintings. Houses -- practically everything was destroyed. I've lived in Beirut for five years, a city that had 15 years of war, and right on the front line the destruction could be bad, but to see a whole town destroyed, this is the first time in my life that I witnessed. But then this did take a inordinate amount of time to take Vukovar, nearly three months. And as I said earlier, day on day, there was heavy shell fire and that's what it causes. And on the 19th of November, we again made contact with the guards units and I went with two of the officers of the guard unit up to the water tower which is -- the sort of the high ground within Vukovar itself, and we went up the water tower, and I recall them saying to me, not me saying to them, but them saying to me, Look we have taken rubble and only rubble.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution wishes to tender 65 ter 04775.3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2336, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. van Lynden, I want to ask you about a meeting that you had in Belgrade with Arkan and Goran Hadzic. In paragraphs 61 to 63 of your statement, you've described having a meeting in a patisserie with Arkan and Goran Hadzic. If you can recall, approximately how long did this meeting last?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Difficult for me to say precisely, but about 45 minutes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And in your statement, you said that Arkan said that all Serbs should be in one state. Had you heard that sentiment expressed by others in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Did you hear that sentiment expressed by anyone that you interviewed in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We had gone to a press conference given by Mr. Seselj in which he expressed that. We had met with various people who we didn't always interview on film but spoke to, and who expressed similar sentiments. And we had interviewed Slobodan Milosevic, at the time president of Serbia, in which he also said that if other republics of the former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were going to become independent, then it was only right that Serbs living in those republics had the right to join Serbia itself and that all Serbs should therefore live in one state.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now in paragraph 62 of your statement you said that after you heard the offer that was being made to you by Arkan and Goran Hadzic, you explained your background to them. What exactly did you share with them about your background?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Maybe I should explain to Their Honours the offer that was made to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, we do have limited time. It's in paragraph 62 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President I want to object. Because, actually, when I look at the statement it doesn't expressly say that the offer was made by both of them. It was made by Arkan. The rest is inference.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: May I rephrase my question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, when you heard the offer that was made, when you were having this meeting with Arkan and Goran Hadzic, you then explained your background to them. Can you explain why you did this and what you shared about your background.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I did that because I was aware before the meeting who Arkan was, that he was a -- leading his own militia and [indiscernible] told me that it is most sensible in those situations to be completely open to them about my own background so that there could be no misunderstandings later. My father was a diplomat. I was married to a diplomat at that time. I had served in the Dutch marine corps. I was in an environment where the people felt that all foreigners were untrustworthy but that it was likely that every foreign journalist was a spy, and, therefore, I thought it simply sensible to explain precisely what my personal background was, which wars I had covered, that I had a military experience, so that it wouldn't be a situation afterwards of Arkan saying, Well, you didn't tell me that you -- we found out now A, B, or C, but I had been completely honest with them beforehand. That's why I explained that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And a moment ago you said that you didn't want to have a situation where after the fact Arkan said, Well, you didn't tell me A, B, or C. What were you concerned would happen if that did take place?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Anything could happen. I could be threatened. I could even be shot or that could happen to my crew. And as a correspondent, one is responsible for one's crew.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I want to ask you about what happened in eastern Croatia after the fall of Vukovar, that is after 20th of November, 1991. And in paragraph 59 of your statement you mentioned that you travelled to eastern Croatia to cover the visit of Mr. Cyrus Vance to the front lines. If you recall, who did he travel with?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: He had Herb Okun, his Chief of Staff, with him, and he came there with -- as I recall with -- with officers from the JNA, from the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If I can ask for Mr. Laugel's assistance, please, to play video 65 ter 05033.5, and this has ERN V000-4593. The clip runs from 17 minutes and 12 seconds to 20 minutes and 21 seconds. And this is a Sky News report, an associated exhibit, and appears at tab 43. I would like to begin this clip at 19 minutes and 10 seconds and play to 19 minutes and 27 seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: "As dusk was falling, Mr. Vance crossed lines again, clearly appalled at what he had seen. "I talked to at least several of the people who had been hit by shell fragments or by some kinds of ammunition ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, can you identify the person speaking to the camera?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This is Cyrus Vance, the former American Secretary of State, speaking and on -- just behind him on the left of the screen is Herb Okun, who served as his Chief of Staff during his mission in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If I could ask Mr. Laugel to continue playing now to 19 minutes and 53 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: "... last four days, which is inconsistent with what I proposed this morning. "From what you've seen, is this really a cease-fire. "Not really, no. And that's what is so disturbing to me, because we simply have to get a cease-fire before one can really seriously talk about deploying a peacekeeping operation in Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, we've just heard Mr. Vance describe that certain places in Osijek had been shelled in recent days. Were you present when he said this?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And during this time-period, including while you were covering this visit of Mr. Vance to the front lines, what did you observe about the adherence by the Serbs to the cease-fire agreement in particular in respect to Osijek where Mr. Vance had just come back from?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, we had one particular day where we had been given permission to go to the front lines outside of Osijek and were then stopped at a certain moment by a Yugoslav officer and he wouldn't let us film. I was there, and Martin Bell was there with his crew. And so we didn't film, but we heard the shelling of Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Indeed, Ms. Clanton. Thank you. Mr. van Lynden, this is the time for our first break. We will take 30 minutes and come back at 11.00. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You have ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, in paragraph 53 of your statement, you describe how after you were in Vukovar on the 18th, 19th, and 20th of November, you a couple of days later put together a video compilation of what you had seen over the course of your time in Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now with the Chamber's leave I would like to show one more video-clip. This video-clip is approximately 16 minutes long, and it contains 1 minute and 10 seconds of footage that we've already seen this morning. But it is part of Mr. van Lynden's compilation about these events. So I would like to show it at this time. It is 65 ter 05033.3. This is part of the individual that bears ERN V000-4593 and this is at tab 39. It runs from 12 seconds to 6 minutes and 38 seconds. The one thing I would like to point out is that the sound quality is not very good for approximately the first 20 seconds, but it does come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: "The last of 100,000 shells, a 100.000 mortar bomb, millions of bullets. For the Croats on Monday, the three-month old battle of Vukovar is lost but not quite over. Die-hard Croat guards holding out, even as hundreds of their comrades and thousands of civilians surrender to the federal army. A long weary column shuffling out of their own town forever. Many are in tears, many in shock or simply in despair "A scene of defeat which silences the victors looking on, perhaps because of the quite nobility with which the Croat fighters lay down their arms. Only for a few is the humiliation too great to bear, but most eyes retain the fine pride of having held out for so long. The following day, the battle over, more inhabitants emerge out of the ruins of Vukovar's town centre. They've survived and leave, dragging their only possessions after them, a slow march to a new existence, the bleak one of refugee. Like almost every other structure, the town's main hospital has been maimed probably beyond repair and yet it hadn't closed, the combines of its basement offering sanctuary to over 500 wounded. Here they'd coped with no electricity, no water, few medicine. Here there had been no privacy but over 30 births and here they try to save even the smallest of lives. "She is six months old and she is very badly wounded here in her leg and she has one little part of shrapnel of the bomb in her stomach and she needs really ... "A better hospital. "Better -- an operation, operation to safe her life. We are doing our best, but I think without transport her in some bigger centre in better condition. It is -- so she will die, I think. "Around the hospital there is an all encompassing stench of death. And the soldiers soon discover why. "An open morgue of those who the hospital staff did not have time to bury. "And with its fall, Vukovar reveals the dark secrets of its war: Its roads, the dead who never reached the hospital or who - the blood still fresh - were clearly murdered. If the ruins of Vukovar symbolise anything at all, it must be the hatred that still exists between the Serbs and the Croats that lain dormant during 45 years of peace, but has now expressed itself in the mutual commitment to war, a commitment which does not appear to have been satisfied even after the three months of fighting here. And amongst the horror there is the surreal incongruity of celebration. Extremist Serb militiamen and women posing triumphantly for an end-of-battle photograph, before returning to a morning feast of music and laughter fueled by alcohol. "The motto on their flag is freedom or death and they vow they will fight on. "No, it's not finished. "What for you do the Serbs need to take before the war is over? "War will be over when we have our limits Karlobag-Karlovac-Ogulin-Virovitica. All place where Serbian people live must be free. You know, we must clean up with the Croatians. "In the town centre, other militiamen display an uncontrolled rejoicing in a similar frame of mind. "But the army's engineers are certainly not celebrating, instead clearing unexploded ordnance or searching for the anti-personnel mines and booby-traps the defenders left behind. To find them is a delicate task, to clear them, less so. "And it takes another day before the wounded of Vukovar can be evacuated, a painful, chaotic exercise. It takes hours before the ambulances have been loaded up. The walking wounded reached the overcrowded buses. And dusk is approaching when the convoy finally departs, taking its occupants on a last site seeing tour of destruction before leaving behind the once beautiful town on the river Danube rendered silent by the victors and the vanquished, lost to its inhabitants and obliterated memorial to hate."

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, in the video-clip that we just saw, I'd like to ask you where the footage was taken in this last shot that should still be on your screen?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: From the top of the water tower.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And is this the same event that you described today earlier? It's on transcript page 32, beginning on line 9 that you went with members of the guards unit to the top of the water tower and they commented on the destruction below them?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. We went up the water tower with two of the officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My name is Christopher Gosnell. I represent Mr. Hadzic here and I'm just going to ask you a few questions today. Am I correct in understanding that you first travelled to Eastern Slavonia in late August or early September 1991?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yup, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you have described today as well as in your statement the distinction that you drew between the northern route and the southern route. Am I right that you visited the north route or the northern area twice or a maximum of three times?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you recall the dates?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not precisely, no. But they would have been in September and -- and October. But thereafter, we only went on the southern route.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So when you say "thereafter," do I understand correctly that the two to three visits to the northern area that occurred at the beginning of your visits to Eastern Slavonia, and then all subsequent visits were along the southern route?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, we did both. For instance, the -- it has been shown in Court the -- my visit to Tovarnik and Ilaca, that would have been in September, but -- and visits to for instance, Brsadin was after that, as far as I recall. So it was a mix.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now you say at paragraph 24 of your statement that you had to obtain -- and can you turn that up in front of you, sir, if you like. You had to obtain permission on a daily basis from the federal Ministry of Defence to enter Eastern Slavonia. Can you explain for us the mechanics of how that occurred?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived -- not immediately when I arrived Belgrade because we did go to -- to Banija and to Knin, but thereafter in August I applied for and received permanent accreditation as a correspondent in Belgrade. And we visited the Ministry of Defence and spoke to their spokesman, whoever was in charge of the press department, and he told us that we would -- if we wanted to go to the front line we would need to get a daily permission from him. Thereafter it wasn't necessary for me to turn up in person. But my field producer, Zoran Kusovac, would go, who had been with me at that original meeting -- would go and get the piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do I understand your last answer to mean that you didn't need this piece of paper from the federal Ministry of Defence when you were going to Banija and Knin but you did need it when you were entering Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: When we -- sorry. When we had originally gone to Bihac, it was, where we based ourselves, we were working -- I was working then with Zoran Kusovac as my field producer but with a crew from Belgrade television and what we needed then was a pass to -- to get into the town of Dvor Na Uni, and with the catch-22 being that you had to be in the town before -- to get the pass and, of course, you couldn't get the pass if you hadn't entered the town yet, but there was also a procedure, although, at that time, as I recall, it was Territorial Defence forces who were imposing that system rather than the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And coming back to Eastern Slavonia, once you have this piece of paper that you have obtained from the federal Ministry of Defence how would that be inspected when you arrived at a check-point?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We would show it, and we would show -- I would show my press accreditation. And on the southern route, as I've explained earlier, we would pass through Sid first, pass office that had been set up there, and it depended on -- on the people manning the check-point whether we were or were not allowed to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And there was a JNA check-point on that bridge at Erdut; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I remember it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did they, likewise, examine the passes that you obtained from the federal Ministry of Defence in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were you asked to show this pass every time that you passed through either the check-point at the Erdut bridge or the check-point north of Sid?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Again, as far as I remember, yes. And -- but there were more check-points north of Sid. I mean, you could -- there was one before Tovarnik but there could be others along the road, and you could be stopped and sent back at any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were those all JNA check-points, as you headed north from Sid into Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in the northern route, did you ever come across check-points in the interior after you had crossed the bridge in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not that I can recall at this time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When you entered the territory, whether in the south or the north, did you to have a JNA escort with you, or were you permitted to drive on your own?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, we didn't have to have to a JNA escort. There were moments, and two of them have been shown in court this morning, both when we were taken to Ilaca and when we were taken to the JNA garrison in the southern part of Vukovar that we were told that the only safe way would be to go in an armoured car and General Arandjelovic then arranged that. But, on the whole, we just went on our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 04677, please, which is Defence tab 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, you testified in the Mrksic case before the Tribunal, and I'd like to show you a passage from your testimony, and this is page 3152 of the transcript, please. And I'm interested in that passage from line 11 onwards, where you say -- and you're referring here to the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You say: "I did not get an impression that their conduct was anything other than as professional soldiers. What for me I observed is that they were quite different to the other units of the JNA that I had encountered and the various militias, specifically, Mr. Seselj's people, that had also been allowed into the front lines of Vukovar by the JNA." And what I'm interested in, sir, is that last bit. Can you explain to us why you say that Mr. Seselj's people had been allowed onto the front lines by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was my impression then that if the JNA had decided that they were completely going to fight this battle on their own without the help of any militia, that they could have been in a position to do so. And, therefore, that the presence of paramilitary groups meant that the JNA had given them permission to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And why do you say that the JNA was in a position to do so?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was a full army and had at its disposal all the weaponry of an army. As far as I'm aware, was one of the biggest, bigger armies, and therefore, at least in my impression, it was that they could have, if they so wished, they should -- could have stopped paramilitary units from being in those areas, but that they had given them permission. Whether that was on the part of the army or a political decision, that, of course, I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And was it also because it was your impression that the JNA controlled the two exclusive access points to Eastern Slavonia where you found Seselj's men, amongst other militia?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Indeed. As you say, yes, they -- they manned the check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When you passed through the check-points, did you ever see militia passing through the check-points?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's a hard question to ask 22 years on. I'm -- I -- I may have done, but it certainly didn't make an impression on me that I have a clear memory of that happening, no [Realtime transcript read in error "yeah"].

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's entirely fair, Mr. van Lynden, I do understand that. And the observation that you made about Seselj's men, namely, that they'd been allowed onto the front lines by the JNA, would you make the same observation about Arkan's militia?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Can I just go to -- there is a mistake. It says a "yeah" when I said a "no" earlier just before your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
