utterances.text: Okay. I visited Arkan's militia in or around Erdut when there was a base, and they were there, so they must have been allowed across the bridge by the JNA. But, here, I am making an assumption, because I did not actually see them crossing the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you recall how many check-points you had to go through between the Croatian border north of Sid before you arrived in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Precise number, no. What I do remember is that the situation changed. I mean, what could happen on one day, the next day might not be the same, that there wouldn't be a check-point. But there were certainly a couple for us to get through, and certainly, as I recall, in Oriolik which is basically the village where one turned right to drive on to Negoslavci and to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can we go back just four pages on the document on the screen now to page 3148. If we can just start down at the bottom of this page. And, again, Mr. van Lynden, this is your testimony --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- from Mrksic, and starting at line 22 you were asked this question: "About your travels from Belgrade to Vukovar and the other way around, you said today that you needed to obtain a permit in Belgrade but that despite this sometimes you were not allowed into the Vukovar area. Can you perhaps remember who was it specifically that denied you access on particular occasions and did you ever have an opportunity to bring this up with superior levels of the army, if the army was the body in question? " And your answer was: "It was at army check-points that we were stopped, and without them giving us precise reasons told that we could not go further." And then if we go down that paragraph you say: "On another occasion, the general had told me that the convoy would take place and that we were stopped in Negoslavci and that a lower officer of the JNA told us that the convoy would not take place and that we would [sic] -- could not go any further ... that day. "If we were stopped on other days, it was generally at check-points and generally not by officers but by possibly a sergeant in the army and we were simply told that we could not go any further despite the fact that we had been given a permission ..." Now, what I'm interested in here, am I correct in understanding that -- well, let me put it a different way. Do you recall whether you were ever stopped at a non-JNA check-point and denied permission to proceed?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not that I recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were JNA forces very concerned about infiltration by Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I'm the right person to ask that question. You should ask someone from the JNA. The only comment that I can make about that is that we were surprised throughout our time in going to Vukovar that we would take this -- the same road -- if we were talking the southern route, Your Honours, it was Tovarnik, Ilaca, Oriolik, and Negoslavci and to Vukovar, that between Tovarnik and Oriolik, the flanks of the road were fields of corn, and what would happen, and it happened to us as well, and we were told also by JNA soldiers that it was happening to them on a routine basis is that Croat snipers would go into those corn fields with some steps, go up the steps, and take one shot at a passing car and go down again and -- and -- and go away. And one of the things for me which was strange was that flank of that road which was of clear importance to the Serb forces that those flanks were not cleansed and held so that such attacks couldn't take place. But that is the only answer I can give to this question. As to how concerned the JNA was or was not you would have to ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When you say they would go up some steps, do you mean that they had some kind of a ladder or stepladder from which they would snipe towards the road?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That is what we were told. Obviously I never saw them, nor were we ever shown any steps that had been captured. But that's what we were told.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were you shot at on a number of occasions by such snipers?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, there were a number of occasions that we heard shots fired. Our cars were never hit. We always travelled in two Volkswagen Golfs, unarmoured, and it seemed to us that we were being shot at, so we heard the bullets relatively close. But none of the cars were ever hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you remember, and I know it's been a very, very long time, Mr. van Lynden, but can you remember the direction from which the fire was coming? Was it coming only from the direction of Vukovar, or was there infiltration coming from the other direction, namely, from the west?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The incidents that I'm referring to are talking place south of Vukovar, and, therefore -- I haven't got the map in front of me, but, yes -- [Overlapping speakers] ... west.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... let's bring up a map. It might help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have D38, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, could we clarify. The last question was: Was there infiltration coming from the other direction. And the first part of the question was if you remembered -- if you could recall which direction the fire was coming from. Could we clarify for the witness if infiltration and fire are the same thing in counsel's question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's start with the fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: For the record, this is Defence tab 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: First of all, I should ask you, Mr. van Lynden, looking at this map, does this accord with your -- and I suggest that if you look at that map it shows that as a certain date the northern area is not accessible from the southern area, and vice versa. Does that accord with your recollection, certainly in September 1991, that you couldn't pass from the northern area to the southern area and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, you couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And I realise that this is not a perfect map, but we can see there generally the direction between Sid and Vukovar. And the question that I was -- was wondering about is, as you're travelling north, north-west, along the road from Sid towards Vukovar, do you remember whether the sniping, either that you experienced or you heard about, was it coming from the west of that road?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Would you like me to mark it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No need to mark it --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: South-west is what I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The fire was coming from the south-west?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That is as what I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we please have 05030 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I would like to have a clarification here. Would that mean, Mr. van Lynden, that travelling in the -- you said you were travelling from -- to Vukovar; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Towards Vukovar. And the sniping came from the corn fields besides next to the road.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very close to the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Close to the road. Now you say they come from south-west?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I mean, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That is left in the direction you were driving.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Left when we were going to Vukovar, on our right when we were coming back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Coming back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And you could also get shot on the way back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes, of course. But now we know which side of the road it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, Mr. van Lynden, if I can just follow up on that, as a military man, would you have expected -- you said that you were surprised that the corn fields were not razed. Would you have considered to be a legitimate and normal military practice to in fact to burn down, raze those corn fields to make the area safer for the military?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure I would have expected them to burn them down. I would have expected them to either to see to it that there is harvesting or simply that there are units further out on the flanks to see to it that this road which it seemed to me was fairly vital for the JNA did not come under sporadic sniper attack. It was never meaningful attack but there were these sniper attacks, and that makes everybody feel uncomfortable. Certainly made us feel uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The reason why I asked you about burning down is because the word that you use at paragraph 26 of your statement and I'll put it in context: "I was surprised to learn that the JNA which was a professional army had not protected its flanks by razing the corn fields."

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: What I meant was a clearing. If I can give a direct example from my past. When the Israeli army invaded Lebanon in 1982, quite soon they -- usually with bulldozers, they didn't burn it, they -- bulldozers. Saw to it that -- specifically in southern Lebanon on the sides of the roads there was often banana groves, things of that sort, but they were cleared so that there was less chance of their forces of being attacked on the road. And I would have expected the JNA to undertake something of a similar nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You say would you expect that. Is that based on your training as a professional military officer?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. That is based on my experience in wars. I spent a lot of time in Lebanon. I was in Iraq an Iran. I was with the American forces during the Gulf War. This is what I've seen professional military forces do, and I was surprised that it did not happen in Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And when you used the word "professional," you mean armed forces acting appropriately both from a strategic perspective and from a laws of war perspective; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure it's called -- it would be called "strategic perspective." It's simply from the perspective of keeping one's own forces as safe as possible. As far as the laws of war are concerned I'm not an expert on whether the razing of corn fields constitutes a crime of war. I would doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: As a military officer it is what you would have done, if you were in that situation. You would have razed the corn fields; correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I have never been put in that situation. When I served in the marine corps we were not at war, and I imagine I would have got orders, received orders and we were -- I was -- simply served in the infantry, not the kind of unit that would have undertaken such an action. That would have been done by engineers, I imagine. But I have never been personally put in a position like that when I was in the marine corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I like to play a video now which is 05030. It's Defence tab 28. And we're starting at 16:45.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "Realise as does their general the kind of war they'll be engaged in. "It's a dirty war in which most of the action is done by snipers and ambushes along the road, surprise attacks during the night. "And the men ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now you've told us that is General Arandjelovic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is that right that what he conveyed to you was that there were attacks -- the primary nature of the attacks against his forces were by snipers and ambushes at night?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That is indeed what he -- he told us during this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we move forward to 17:06, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "To get to one of the general's front lines an armoured personnel carrier is put at our disposal, the men on guard against the ambushes they say are a standard part of every late afternoon. We drive to Ilaca ... "

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were you told that these ambushes were so regular that they were a standard part of every late afternoon?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's what I just said, so, yes, I must have been.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: "... are there, houses are still burning and the army's control tentative. The village of Nijemci and the electrical pylons delineate the front line just one mile away. But the army here complains of constant infiltration by the Croats. For the officers it is frustrating. As one put it, there's no truce ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Just stop there for one moment. The individual behind you in the fatigues, can you say what force he is a part of?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: He's a member of the JNA. Whether he's full-time or reservist, that I can't tell. Probably a reservist. But ...

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: "No war that we have our hands tide by a cease-fire agreement. On these front lines they haven't had time to dig in yet and its anti-aircraft guns which form the primary defence against the snipers that the night is bound to bring. "Aernout van Lynden, Sky News."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, somewhere in that report you said that the army's control is tentative. And why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This is about Ilaca which they had only just taken where the houses were still burning and where their control was therefore tentative. They -- this was clear from the demeanour of the men, weary of some kind of a counter-attack. That never happened, as far as I'm aware, but they were very uncertain still.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did they tell you that Croat forces were moving through this area attempting to resupply Vukovar? In particular, using the cover of the corn fields.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. That's not something that I remember being told. I remember being told that there were instances of sniping and of ambushes but I don't remember being told that this was a primary route to resupplying the Croat forces in Vukovar itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 05033, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And excuse me, if it would assist, the previous clip was 65 ter was 05030.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I thank you my friend for that. And just for the record my understanding, and I believe my friend has confirmed this, that the entire video has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Each sub65 ter which is each clip, so from start to finish of his report has been admitted for all of the ones that are associated exhibits. It is possible that on the longer video which is the V000-plus the four digits there is additional clips that do not relate to his coverage in eastern Croatia and thus were not part of the 92 ter statement. But everything that was in the statement has now been tendered in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My wish would be to tender the entire video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would need to check. But for each video I'm not certain at this time if everything on that video relates to this part of the conflict. This witness has a considerable amount of video related to Western Slavonia and also to Bosnia and sometimes it's mixed in. Perhaps during the break if I would be allowed to check to see if there's any parts of the video, the whole video that -- don't relate, that might save Your Honours from having evidence that doesn't cover this part of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I have reviewed the video and I recall no coverage of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just want to look. Having reviewed many of these videos. Some of them have different parts of the conflict and the reason we created the sub65 ters was to have each report as a distinction exhibit for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You'll come back to us right after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes, can I do that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can we have 05033, at 6 minutes 40 seconds. This is Defence tab 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "The guns of Western Slavonia are silent. Deployed in fields that have turned into swamps, most stand deserted, only one crew venturing through the mud ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall going to Western Slavonia yourself?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In the Autumn of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would this have been included in your two to three visits that you say occurred to the north area? In other words did you travel through the northern area to get there, or did you go by some other route?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, we went via Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "... check the sites. For the soldiers, the unexpected truce offers an unexpected respite. The war of Western Slavonia has either been fought at close range, snipers infiltrating each other's line, or at long range with heavy artillery. And this is the first day in months that the gun crews have not been given the order to fire. The villages in the Western Slavonia offer by now the depressingly familiar site of homes and restaurants holed by shell fire, raked by bullets or simply burned out. But even after the army captured them the Croat forces attack on an almost daily basis infiltrating through the region's ample woods."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Does that remind that you that at least in Western Slavonia there was a considerable amount of infiltration by Croat forces across Serbian lines?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It's a war and a war is being fought and this is what we were being told by the JNA in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We would tender this video, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is it the entire video you're tendering, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's my intention, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would again ask for a moment, please, during the break to confirm what else is on this video. As just discussed we broken it apart and we tendered it that way. But I can check the entire video if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So that makes two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can we go back, please, to 05030, again Defence tab 28. We're going to time mark 11:49.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We have not been provided with the transcript of the video which makes interpretation really difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry about that. I indeed do not have the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "... that Yugoslavia cease-fires's is not holding. From the front line, first aid posts, the wounded continued to emerge. The current truce may have halted the offensives but it doesn't stop the shooting, although these federal soldiers were wounded by their own fire rather than by that of their foes. It happened on the army's front line around the eastern Croatian town of Osijek and the brigade commander goes out to investigate, although the only explanation he ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you recognise this person?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: A brigade commander. I can't remember his name. We encountered him on one day as we've just heard outside on the front outside Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, again, I know it's been an extremely long time. Do you have any recollection of whether there was a village nearby?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. Because that's where those two men who had -- there had been an incident with -- as I recall, a recoilless rifle and some anti-tank -- anti-tank bazooka, and they had been standing behind it and a flame comes out and they'd both been burnt. And they were initially brought to that village. I cannot remember the name of the village today. And from there, by hospital, they were -- by ambulance they were taken to hospitals. I imagine within Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: "Lack of discipline when this recoilless rifle was fired, perhaps indicative of the strange mixture to be found amongst the men who manned the army's trenches. Some are professionals, some of short-term volunteers ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you recognise the symbol on that helmet?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It's sort of national symbol of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Does it tell you anything about the affiliations of this soldier?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It would seem to indicate that he is affiliated to the nationalist side.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: "Others barely trained conscripts. Although the fortifications include an unlikely variety of heavy weapons, 50-year-old American artillery, modern Russian anti-tank rockets, the men remain continually vigilant. Since the cease-fire, they say, they have come under attack on 56 separate occasions. For these men and their mortars in the front line trenches the firing has never ceased, only diminished, but during the past 48 hours the violations have significantly increased leading many of the soldiers here to believe that Yugoslavia's sixth cease-fire is about to break down."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Those men over your right shoulder, can you identify their unit affiliations?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not their precise unit, no, but they were members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And over your left shoulder there is a different uniform. It is more of a camouflage. Is that also a uniform would you associate with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I would. The guy was the personal - how would you call it? - body-guard of the brigade commander. We've seen him earlier as -- when I talk about a professional. So I imagine that here on the one hand you have reservists and, on the other hand, a professional within -- both within the JNA forces.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: "... completely. Even amongst the men deployed away from the front lines, overlooking the wine yards and the farm houses, that opinion is standard. For the moment they have the time for haircuts, for makeshift showers, or leisurely chats in the shade, but few doubt they will soon be otherwise engaged. "In my opinion, war is not over. "And if it isn't, these tanks dug in 8 kilometres from Osijek will be thrown into the fray. Their muzzles no longer silent. "Aernout van Lynden, Sky News."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, am I right that all of that artillery, the heavy artillery we see in the tanks, is that mixed in near where the infantry is?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, not the artillery. And actually not the tanks either. These tanks were quite away behind the front lines. What we saw there was some pieces of -- of -- what we call self-propelled artillery on the front line, but most of the tanks that I've seen and certainly most of the artillery is kept kind the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And can you recall was that brigade commander inspecting the trench where we saw that variety of -- that assortment of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would you say he was in command of all those people, based on what you were able to observe?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We were only there for a few hour, but, yes, our impression was that he was in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I've already tendered this document and I know it's -- this video I know it's under consideration by the Prosecution but I'm done with that document, that video. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. van Lynden, I'd now like to ask you some questions about the meeting that you say that you -- and I believe you'd like some water if the usher to please assist. About the meeting that you say you had with Arkan and Mr. Hadzic. Now, can I first ask you, do you remember whether that meeting happened before or after your first trip to Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: After, as far as I remember. Putting a precise timeline on it is difficult for me. I've obviously thought about this, also in preparation of coming here today. The meeting sticks in my mind because it was completely different to anything else I have experienced during my life. But the precise timing on it, I don't know. But it was certainly in September 1991. But I couldn't give you a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And please tell us how this meeting started. How did it come about that you ended up at the patisserie, starting from you being at your hotel.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I -- I think it's described in -- in my statement, my producer, my field producer and I had met in Belgrade a character whom we had considered shady but who said he had good connections and he spoke English. And on this particular night I had gone to bed. As I recall, it was around 1.30 in the morning that I was called, and reception called saying there was someone downstairs in reception wishing to collect me, or to speak to me, and he spoke to me, and said that I should come down for what he described as an important meeting. One is then faced with a strange decision. My field producer had his own apartment in Belgrade, so I would have had to go on my own, and it's one of those situations where, in a foreign country where fighting has started, you take a decision should I or shouldn't I? I decided to take a risk and to go. And I came downstairs and he was waiting, and as I recall in camouflage combat gear, but before I had met this man only in civilian clothes. He was carrying a Heckler & Koch submachine-gun with a silencer on it, and he motioned for me to come with him. Outside the hotel there was a BMW with a driver in it, also in camouflage clothes, and, as I recall, the BMW had Frankfurt number plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can I just stop you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And could we have 04678, which is Defence tab 168. If we could please have transcript page 3210.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we look at line 21, it says -- and this is your testimony from the Mrksic case.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "And a man who had met with my field producer earlier that week and who spoke English asked me to come down because there was an important meeting for him to take me to." Do you remember, was it just your field producer who had met this man or had you previously met this man as well?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I had previously met this man as well, on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You say you were already in bed. How long did it take you to get down to the lobby, approximately?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: A couple of minutes. I just put my clothes on. I didn't shower or shave or anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Two minutes to get all your clothes on and get down into the lobby looking at least semi-presentable?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Shirt, trouser, I mean how long does that take.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then you arrive in the car. Did you say that the driver was wearing camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's what I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was he armed?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How could you say he was armed? Did you see him with his weapon?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: There was -- I mean, he was driving but there was a separate gun, as I recall, by the passenger chair.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you sit in the back seat?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did the man who had retrieved you at the hotel, did he also sit in the back seat?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I recall, he sat in the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how long did it take to you drive from the hotel to the patisserie?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't have a precise recollection of how long it took. But we were in new Belgrade. It would have taken a little while, but I don't have a precise recollection as to how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember that Arkan's patisserie was near the stadium, the football statement?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing a stadium on that drive. I never went to the patisserie before or after. I had heard of its existence but that was all. And it was at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say it took at least ten minutes to drive from the hotel to the patisserie?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I would think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You say at paragraph 61: "When we got out, I saw about 40 men similarly dressed in western camouflage, carrying heavy machine-gun, rifles and anti-tank bazookas." Now, first of all, can I just ask you about their attire. Were they, would you say, well presented, professionally presented or were they unkempt?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: They seemed to me well attired, certainly not unkempt. It was dark. It was something of a surprise. My basic reaction at that time was that I had made an enormous error in not bringing my cameraman because I thought that what I was seeing was some sort of a coup was going to be stagged. That turned out not to be the case. But that was my initial reaction. No, they were well attired and appeared at ease with their weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And can you just describe that scene for us, please. What were they doing? Were they waiting for something? Was there a vehicle nearby that they were going to get into? Were they just standing there, milling about?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, I was wondering the same thing, what were they doing there. I didn't know, nor was there any time for me to ask. I was brought straight from the car, passed these men who were standing in the street. If there were trucks waiting to take them away, I don't recall that. There may have been, I don't remember. And I was taken into the patisserie.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then you say here at paragraph 61: "After a short while, Arkan walked with Goran Hadzic." How long would you say, carrying on with our chronology, was a short while?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: A couple of minutes. I was offered a drink. I asked for a coffee and a water. I think I was given a coffee and a water prior to their arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You say here at paragraph 61: "I did not know Goran Hadzic at that time." Does that mean that you had never heard of him as of that meeting, or does it mean that you had merely never made his acquaintance but you had heard of him?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I had never made the acquaintance of either of the two gentlemen. I had heard of Arkan. Zeljko Raznjatovic, to give him his formal name. I had not heard, I was not aware of Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You said earlier that this meeting occurs after your first visit to Eastern Slavonia. Do I understand correctly that it was after a visit to the northern route?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That I can't remember, whether it was before or after -- no, I don't -- that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you recall that your earliest transcripts to Eastern Slavonia, in general, were, in fact, to the northern area?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. We did one in the north, we did one in the -- several in the south. So, no. I'm certainly aware of doing -- it must have been two after this meeting in the northern area. So I may have done one beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then further on in paragraph 61 you say: "Arkan said they would give me, and through me my network, exclusive rights to cover the war in Eastern Slavonia." Now, you've described to us the process by which you, in fact, were granted access to Eastern Slavonia and, as I understand it, there was no involvement of Arkan in that process, or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, you're not wrong. As I also write here, I was -- or write, said: "I was very surprised." And I was very surprised. I think it was the last thing I was possibly expecting. This has never happened to me anywhere, in any war zone. I was flabbergasted, really, also, because to make an offer like that to a western journalist, no western journalist is ever going to accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At this point Arkan must have known -- or, well, I can just ask you, did it appear from your interaction with him that he knew you had already visited Eastern Slavonia as of that date, as of the date of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I do not recall either of them saying anything about my coverage of Eastern Slavonia. What I do recall is that they mentioned coverage I had done earlier in the Banija area, the towns of Glina, Dvor Na Uni that I mentioned earlier. I remember that they mentioned that. They may have mentioned other reports that I did, but that I don't recall at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I suppose what I'm getting at is, did you have the impression that Arkan considered you to be an astoundingly gullible person? And I ask that question because he must have known that you were at least somewhat well informed about how to get access to Eastern Slavonia, and yet here he is attempting to use that as some kind of a bargaining chip to obtain night-vision equipment.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I always had the impression, and in thinking back on this incident, always thought it was more -- he wasn't just there talking to me about getting night-vision equipment. I think what he -- and I imagine Mr. Hadzic agreed with him because he was sitting next to him and was with him when he made this offer. That they thought that I would give the kind of coverage of the war that they would like. And they felt that I would, to a degree, let's say, support what they were doing. So I think it was more about press relations rather than about getting equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Aside from Mr. Hadzic and Arkan, was anyone present during your meeting with them?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: There may have been a waiter there, but no one else, as far as I remember. And also not the man who brought us -- who brought me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did Mr. Hadzic speak at all during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I do not remember him speaking to me in English. They spoke to each other, but in Serbo-Croat, which is a language I don't speak. I don't recall Mr. Hadzic asking me a question directly. I -- what I recall is that it was Arkan who did most of the talking with me, and he did speak English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was Mr. Hadzic present throughout what you've described earlier as a 45-minute meeting? Was he present throughout?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That is my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can we go --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: They left together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to 04678, Defence tab 16. Could we please turn to 3211.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Here's what you said, Mr. van Lynden, during your testimony in Mrksic starting at line 12: "I was given a cup of coffee and then Mr. Raznjatovic, together with Goran Hadzic, entered the room, and we had a meeting lasting, I don't know, I can't remember precisely, 30 or 40 minutes. Mr. Raznjatovic was the one speaking. He spoke relatively good English. As far as I recall, Mr. Hadzic speak English at all." Does it appear to you there's a word missing from what you said during your testimony in the Mrksic case?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It does not speak English at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then the next sentence you say: "So the conversation was very much between Mr. Raznjatovic and myself and that was the first meeting I had with these two gentlemen."

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is that all true?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: None that of that appears in your statement that has been tendered to the Court as your testimony.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: What is missing in my statement that has been tendered to the Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: There is no mention in your statement that the conversation was very much between you and Mr. Raznjatovic. There's no mention that you did not recall that Mr. Hadzic spoke or that he spoke in English?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic didn't speak in English to me, as far as I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If I could assist by directing counsel to paragraph 61 where it says that "Hadzic did not speak much." I think that relates to the point you've just made with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, why don't you -- I don't know if you have in front of you, do you have paragraph 61 there in front of you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would you agree there appear to be some details at least in terms of your recollection that are not recorded there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't recall Mr. Hadzic speaking much. He certainly -- I don't recall him speaking to me. I don't recall him speaking in English. I recall Arkan doing most of the talking and that he spoke reasonable English, fluent might be a bit strong. I recall him saying that they both liked the work I had done in Glina and Knin, as I've just said. I recall them making me that offer so I'm not quite sure what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we'll get to that after the break, Mr. President. Mr. van Lynden, this is the time for our second break, 30 minutes as well. So that means we'll come back at 12.45. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Did you finish your -- the two video.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Indeed, we were able to look at both videos and to see which parts had been used with the witness before and which parts were also not related to the evidence that this witness has for this case. As a general matter, we would not agree to admission of these videos just because they're van Lynden footage. The witness hasn't had an opportunity to see all of the video-clips that are contained in the entire video that the Defence counsel has offered to tendered. And before he could be used to tendered that video he would have to be able to review those clips. Also the Prosecution hasn't been able to revue all of those parts when they are not identified at specific time codes. Because I am familiar with these videos and because they do form part of his evidence I did go back and look at the two particular videos that are dealt with. One of them, now that Defence counsel has shown Mr. van Lynden a segment on Western Slavonia, that entire video is now covered in terms of those reports have been shown to the witness and are part of his evidence. Every other segment is part of his 92 ter and it has got a sub65 ter. So for that one, we propose that if the Defence wishes to tender the footage on Western Slavonia that they tender just that time code and give that a sub65 ter in order that we wouldn't have overlap between what has been admitted as an associated exhibit and what is going in with the Defence request for that portion of the video. For the other video which is 05030, there are several --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Being the second one or the first one we are discussing about.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I believe it is the second one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Second one. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: The second one that was shown the witness, the part that was shown is not the only part that was not shown to him before and not part of his evidence. There are several other news reports in that video that spans 40 minutes that cover topics that have not come up with the witness that we have not shown to him and have not been shown to him by Defence counsel. So at this time we would say they are not appropriate for admission. These are events that happened in other parts of Croatia or other matters related to the developments at that time that aren't part of this case, so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, my understanding at least as far as 05030 goes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I think -- I think it's the second one, even though it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So this is the one that apparently the Prosecution has a particular problem with. Now my understanding and I may be wrong, but I understood that all of this footage was prepared or in some way associated with Mr. van Lynden's work and I don't know how it was put together but the reason why I wish to tender it as a whole is because there does appear to be some kind of a sequence. I don't know how the sequence was put together. I'm not sure if the Prosecution put it together or if Mr. van Lynden had anything to do with that. But we leave that the entire video should be tendered to provide that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What I would suggest is that, for the time being, we MFI it. Parties come together and discuss -- discuss it, see whether they can solve the problem, and come back to us either with agreement or with a request for the Trial Chamber to take the decision. So let's ... let's MFI both of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 05030 shall be given Exhibit D86, marked for identification. And 05033 will become D87, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just to clarify, please, the parts of these videos that are associated exhibits, the statement, would not be affected by Your Honours' decision to MFI the remaining parts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, we apologise for the little delay. We had a technical matter to discuss. Mr. Gosnell, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. van Lynden, at paragraph 63 of your statement you say: "To guarantee exclusive access meant that he," meaning Arkan, "was able to control access to the area and presumably prevent other journalists from entering. This kind of control would require the agreement of the military and local authorities." Can I, first of all, ask you what did you mean when you used the expression "local authorities" here?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Local authorities, I meant that from my experience specifically, actually on the northern route, there were Territorial Defence forces, as those who had taken me to Brsadin and showed me Brsadin as we saw earlier today. So that's really what I was referring to there, rather different to the JNA as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: From your observation, were they under the command of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I did not see them on that visit to Brsadin as being under the control of the JNA. They may have, but from what I saw on that visit, they appeared to be under their own control.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And during that other visit that we saw the footage of when you were at the front line and we saw a variety of uniforms, would you say that on that occasion you observed that the Territorial Defence was under the control of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure at that -- that at that point - this is outside Osijek that you're referring to - that I saw Territorial Defence soldiers there. As far as I am aware, there were reservists and they were professionals and they certainly all came under the command and control of the brigade commander who we saw in that footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How would you distinguish between Territorial Defence reservists and militia, let's say?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Different ways. Firstly, in the kind of clothes they wore. For instance, if you look at the footage at Brsadin, you see people also wearing jeans. So there is the clothing. With the reservist, who were often in full JNA clothes but their hair was longer, they had clearly just been called up, and with militia, they had all sorts of different insignia, and, lastly, through whatever Zoran was telling me because he was talking to these people and was able to give me more information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So your impression in terms of uniforms was that green khaki would be reservists, and it would not be Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It could be either, but in that case it was often what we were told on the ground as to what people were. My memory and I think my words in that report from Brsadin bears it out is that we were told at that time that these were Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Further along in paragraph 63 you say: "Since this was the offer made by Arkan and Hadzic, a political leader, I figured that they worked together and had agreed that they could actually effect this. Arkan and Hadzic were comfortable with each other and were working together as close allies." Am I correct that that observation on your part is based upon your experience at the patisserie meeting them?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Basically, yes. We did meet them again in Erdut but for much shorter meetings. But this was my impression from that meeting in Belgrade, basically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You say you met them together again?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In Erdut, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And when and where did that occur?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: After this occasion. We passed by -- because I had been there on my own I also wanted to introduce my field producer to both gentlemen, also because I wouldn't be the only correspondence covering this war and I would -- usually the deal was that I would do 60 days and then would be given a number of days off and somebody else would come in from London, and therefore I felt it was important for Zoran to have met them and he did. My recollection is that we went past an offices and met Mr. Hadzic there and that we were collected from that office by Arkan and then taken to his training facilities or camp, whatever it was, and we were there for not that long. About -- at that camp, for, I don't know, 30 minutes, and then we went on our way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So the time that you see Arkan and Mr. Hadzic together in one another's presence, is when Arkan comes and picks you up from Mr. Hadzic's office. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And about how long was that overlap when they were both together and you were there with them?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't have a precise recollection of time, but probably not very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And can you recall what was said, if anything, that you could understand?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: They spoke in Serbo-Croat, and I have no precise recollection of anything that was said at the time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So the claim in your statement that they were close allies, your understanding that they were close allies, was based on the patisserie meeting and this interval when Arkan comes and takes you from Mr. Hadzic's office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. And in the -- the way that they appeared to get on together when I saw them. I had no reason to doubt -- also because they had called this meeting, not the other way around. I didn't ask to see them, they asked to see me. And they had done that together. That led me to the conclusion that they were in close touch with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You used the word allies.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Allies, yes. What's wrong with the word allies? I mean, they were on the same side in the same war. That makes them allies in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 04678, Defence tab 16, please. And could we please go to 32:12.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. van Lynden, this passage is from your cross-examination during the Mrksic case by Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And I would like to contextualise your answer with the question, starting at line 3: "Q. You've been around. You have toured many front lines. You have met many warriors. We are talking now about Goran Hadzic and Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. I would like to know what you believed their relationship to be like, their mutual relationship. Did they trust each other? Was there perhaps a certain amount of dissidence between them? Just your impression, based on your impression of their behaviour in your presence. "A. It is purely an impression, but it seemed that the two were at least politically of one view. It seemed to me that the two men were quite different. One was a man who did not hide the fact that he led a militia and that he was comfortable with guns and with killing, and the other man, at least in my impression, was more of a political figure that is to say, or us say, not a military figure. How close or not they were was very difficult for me to say in one meeting, where most of the conversation was only with one of them because I couldn't have a conversation with the other, as we didn't have a common language." Now do you stand by that testimony?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yeah. The basis, what I'll saying here -- I mean here today and what I said then was, of course, it is based on the impression of one meeting. The two men were different. One was a man who led a militia. And the other appeared to me to be a political leader. But my impression was that they were very comfortable with each other and that they were political allies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did Mr. Hadzic express any political views during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not that I recall, nor do I recall -- well, the one thing that I do recall from this meeting, aside from their offer and then a discussion about my personal background and Mr. Raznjatovic telling me that he didn't take prisoners and that if he took me along he wouldn't let me film the killing of any prison that he took, was that I was told that there was going to be a new Serb army, and -- different from the current JNA, a proper Serb army. And that they were both in agreement that that should happen. When I left that meeting and when I was driven away, I wasn't driven back to the hotel I was taken to a villa without any explanation where there was an older man who also, again, who spoke English and who again spoke about the founding of a new Serbian army. As they had sent me to this man, I imagine that they held similar views. Why else take me to the villa, to this -- I mean, by that time it was pretty late at night, the meeting with this man. So that led me -- that is the only thing about the political views that I could add.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You say in your testimony in Mrksic: "We didn't have a common language," referring you to and Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were you able to say how much Mr. Hadzic was able to understand of your conversation with Mr. -- with Arkan?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: You would have to ask him that. But he appeared completely comfortable with the conversation that Arkan was having with me. I do not recall if Arkan was translating everything. I suspect not. And how much he understood or did not understand, that is not for me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can we now look, please, at paragraph 65 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar [sic]. And you describe your visit to the training centre, Arkan's training centre, or his barracks, as you describe them. And you say: "It was only when I went to his barracks in Erdut that I realised that his troops were all criminals. It was the most extraordinary collection of faces, all bearing scars and wounds and signs of a life in crime. Their characters were clearly not fit for military service. I could see that they were soft-target people, coming in after the army does the hard work, cleaning up, looting ... " Now, is that -- are those conclusions all based on your assessment of their faces?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Basically, yes. We were not there very long. I have been with a lot of military units in my life, with both army and with militias. I have never encountered this kind of collection of faces before. From my experience in Beirut of various militias, there had been somewhere it was clearly more a criminal than a military element, and I compared them to that. And my feeling was that this was a criminal rather than a military unit, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You've told us earlier that when you observed the 40 men in Arkan's militia who were in Belgrade in front of the patisserie that they were well presented. Did you observe the same thing when you went to the barracks in Erdut? Leaving aside their faces.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, I can't leave aside their faces. I couldn't see their faces in Belgrade because they had -- they were wearing full camouflage, and it is their faces which made the deep impression on me when I was in Erdut. As far as their bearing is concerned and the way they wore their uniforms, that was perfectly -- that was -- that looked professional. There was some carrying weapons when I was in Erdut, but a lot of them were not at that moment, which made sense because they were in barracks; whilst in Belgrade they had. And what I saw -- the way they carried their weaponry, they seemed comfortable and professional in that manner. It's -- it's just the faces which I never saw in Belgrade that night that I suddenly did see in Erdut and that's what shocked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you see any other signs that they were -- leaving aside whether they did or didn't commit crimes, did you see signs when you visited the barracks that they were subject to what you would call a professional military discipline?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, there were commanders. I mean, below Arkan. We did not film there. So no, that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that far from coming in behind the army, that actually it was Arkan's unit that was in the front of many attacks in the infantry?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Did I ever hear that? Yes. Did I ever personally witness it? No. I'm also aware of other instances, after this, and specifically in Bosnia, Bijeljina, but also right towards the end of the war in Bosnia, at Sanski Most, that his forces were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did anyone from the JNA talk to you about their relationship, their relationship between the JNA and Arkan's militia?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: There was a - how shall I put it? - a distinct dislike on the part of those that we tried to speak to about the relationship of the JNA with not just Arkan's militia but also, for instance, Seselj's people. Other paramilitary units. And when we asked what is the precise relationship, who is in command, these were uncomfortable questions to which we usually were not given answers by those more senior JNA sources that we had and saw in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Does that mean that you had the sense that they knew Arkan was there but they didn't want to acknowledge that to you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: They certainly knew that Arkan was there. Everybody knew Arkan was there. He was on television. He'd specifically made a great impression when two or three of his men who had been captured and killed by the Croats and had clearly been tortured were returned to them. This is footage that I've seen. And this was shown on Belgrade television and with Arkan making various points, including the point about no longer being willing to take prisoners because of what had happened to his men. So they were absolutely aware of Arkan. They were not just willing to, as I recall, give a detailed explanation as to who commanded who, or how, if he did fall under the orders of the army, how his forces were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I didn't put my question well and I apologise for that. The question I meant to ask you was: That they were, these JNA officials whom you met in Belgrade, that they had placed him in Eastern Slavonia, that they exercised control over him, that they were using him in operations, and they didn't want to acknowledge any of that to you.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That may be the case, but they certainly didn't acknowledge it to me, no. However, I would say, his mere presence there meant that it had to be in connivance with the JNA, that the JNA was clearly -- they knew that he was there and his men was [sic] there and that his barracks were there, and that that could not have been the case if the JNA had not allowed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you know that there was a press conference in December or January, December 1991 or January 1992, where there was JNA general who praised Arkan precisely for his role in JNA operations?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I was not present at the press conference, so, no, I -- I don't -- but no -- back to your original question, I did not get - and these were fairly high sources that we had - anybody saying precisely, He falls under us. We control him. No, they never told us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And based on your observation of the equipment, weapons, vehicles, attire, was there anything from what you observed at the training centre that suggested to you that there was that connection with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I already said, they couldn't be there without there being a JNA connection. Just their mere presence there meant that there had to be a JNA connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I do understand that. But now I'm asking you as somebody with military experience and insight whether, from looking at the weapons, the attire, the vehicles, did any of that suggest that there was a connection between Arkan's militia and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I imagine there was, because, otherwise, why would they have allowed him to have all that material? No, there had to be a direct connection between the two, yes. Although much of the weaponry was western European.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You served for two and a half years in the Royal Dutch Marines; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is there a component of the Royal Dutch Marines that is known as the anti-terrorist unit?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It's not quite called that, but, yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And am I right that they operate, on occasion, with the police, in order to engage in various actions?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Within any anti-terrorist operations, at least in my days - it may have changed since then - the forces comprised of both police and of marines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would you describe this unit as special forces?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. I would describe it as an anti-terrorist unit, in which there are -- there has to be the capability for different capabilities, let us say. For instance, this capability of sniping is not something that we are taught within the Dutch Marine Corps but where you do have police snipers. So that's just the reason for this. The Dutch Marine Corps as a whole, though, would basically be called a special force within the Netherlands. It's small, we're trained as para commandos.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did their equipment include the issuance of balaclavas?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When would they use balaclavas?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: For night operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: As a means of concealment?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 1D576, please, which is Defence tab 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How long were you covering the Gulf War, Mr. van Lynden? By that, I'm referring to the first Gulf War.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: From August 1990 until the end of March 1992 -- 1991. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ever see any Navy Seals of the United States engaging in operations?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were issued with balaclavas as part of their standard equipment?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: They may well be, but I don't know. I've never encountered the Navy Seals.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So I don't suppose looking at this photograph in front of us that you can tell us anything that you recognise.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you know whether French special forces are also issued with balaclavas?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I have never worked with French special forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. Ms. Clanton, anything in re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, this brings your testimony to an end. We thank you very much for assisting the Tribunal. You're now released as a witness. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is there anything else to be discussed? I suppose we don't have another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: He is -- he arrived this weekend for proofing, Mr. President, but our -- our strong preference would be to ask that he begin his testimony tomorrow -- tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It seems reasonable, yes, taking into account how late it -- the time right now. So if there's nothing else, court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on the Tuesday, the 16th day of July, 2013
